summary: Vergecast livestream with David Pierce, Jen Tuohy (smart home reviewer, attended Apple's launch in person) and Nilay Patel reacting to Apple's 'welcome home' launch. Covers the HomeView 7-inch smart display with Siri AI, multi-user face recognition, new Apple TV and HomePod mini, and the LG/Schneider Apple Home collection. Much of the talk is about whether the HomeView should have been an iPad, how multi-user and personal context work in a shared kitchen device, and the price and privacy trade-offs. Ad reads are interspersed and unrelated.
speakers_or_authors: David Pierce, Jen Tuohy, Nilay Patel (The Verge)
relevance_reason: Central to the personal-context and devices theme: a new Apple home device built around Siri AI and personal context, with first-hand demo impressions, multi-user identification, privacy and camera trade-offs, and voice interaction on a shared screen. Mostly demo and launch-event impressions, not long-term use.
themes: Siri AI in the smart home

claims.claim: Apple presented the launch as an 'experience' in a staged townhouse. The display units were in demo mode and could not be controlled, though Jen did get some hands-on time in the apartment space.

HomeView is a 7-inch smart display that recognizes up to six people by camera and switches between them, but only if they have iOS devices. The hosts see multi-user support as the feature that will make or break it.

In Apple's demo video the user is recognized without clearly facing the device, and later a mom has to swivel it toward herself. The hosts question how quickly user switching works and how Siri knows who is speaking. Jen says standing in front of a device to be recognized is a poor experience, based on her Echo Show tests.

Apple introduced an 'unrecognized user' guest mode. Anyone can do things that don't need personal context or security control, such as lights, thermostats, general questions and music. Live streams are viewable but not recordings.

Apple says Siri AI being ready is why it launched the device now. Jen asked whether it could add 'home context' to personal context and says Apple is aiming at 'smart home 101'. She says it is not doing much with AI beyond an extension of the iPhone, though she has tested Home Assistant's AI for a year and sees potential.

The hosts say competitors are launching agent-like tools, and people have built home dashboards with Claude Code to run their smart homes. They argue the automation that makes this stuff valuable is missing from Apple's product.

Apple's LG cameras and sensors reportedly route through Apple devices (home hub, HomeView, Apple TV), not LG servers or apps. Apple pitches this as the privacy and security angle, using HomeKit Secure Video.

New Apple Intelligence features, such as AI text descriptions, on HomeKit Secure Video cameras reportedly require subscriptions up to $60 a month for five cameras. Hosts say camera makers have little incentive to adopt Matter because subscriptions are the business model.

The new $299 Apple TV 4K adds far-field microphones so you can talk to Siri AI directly. The HomePod mini gets the S10 chip, but Siri AI is not available at launch and arrives in a later update. Siri AI on Apple TV is in beta.

Nilay argues that the HomeView would have made more sense three years ago, and that Siri AI arrived too late to bring many people into the smart home. He also says Apple is betting the HomeView becomes people's first smart home device.
Jen says smart home makers have failed to explain benefits and that most people enter via a single-point solution. Apple's pitch is to make that first experience good.

commercial_interest: Verge hosts are not Apple-affiliated. The episode has many unrelated ad reads (AWS, Jira, ServiceNow, Upwork, Framer, Bitwarden, Schwab, Canva, Comcast Business) and an Apple Watch Series 12 ad at the end. Hosts joke about Schneider Electric but disclose no payment.
older_event: No. The Apple HomeView launch event happened the day of the episode and the products ship over the next month. The hosts mention that Apple's HomeKit Secure Video spec was re-architected at WWDC earlier this year.
